The Cr sidewall coating is used in this work as a sacrificial protection layer during DRIE and is removed after release using Chromium Etchant 18 at room temperature with a calibrated overetch margin (Figs. 1i and 2k). In the designed passivation stack, an intermediate SiO2 layer is deposited before Cr sidewall passivation, separating the sacrificial Cr coating from the Si NW sidewalls and minimizing direct Si–Cr contact during release. In addition, since no high-temperature step is performed after Cr passivation, thermally driven Cr transport across the oxide interlayer into the Si NW channel is expected to be negligible. Following Cr wet etching, subsequent HF vapor etching removes oxide from the exposed Si surfaces, including the NW sidewalls.

The complete layer removal is ensured through endpoint detection. Nominally, the recipes used are highly selective: the Cr removal recipe yields a 65–70 nm/min etch rate, and the SiO2 removal recipe yields roughly 50 nm/min, with no measurable SiO2/Cr removal under the applied conditions.
Release of the suspended NW is achieved using Bosch-type DRIE with alternating etch (SF6/O2) and passivation (C4F8) cycles. The isotropic etch component generates the undercut required to release the structure from the bottom surface, forming the suspended Si NW geometry (Fig. 1h). DRIE is performed at the chip level using a carrier wafer, with the platen set to ~1°C. Etching is performed with 5 s of etch and 2 s of passivation cycles to achieve a release depth of 2 µm.

Suspended Si NWs with different dimensions and layouts are fabricated to evaluate the repeatability and robustness of the proposed process (Fig. 3). Figure 3a shows suspended single Si NWs with a CD of 50 nm and AR of 20, 50, and 100, corresponding to NW lengths of \(1\,\mu\mathrm{m}\), \(2.5\,\mu\mathrm{m}\), and \(5\,\mu\mathrm{m}\), respectively. Complete release is achieved across all geometries, indicating reliable transfer from preform definition to the final suspended structure. Even at AR = 100, the NWs exhibit no visible sagging, buckling, or deformation, confirming structural integrity and effective sidewall protection during DRIE. The consistent undercut observed in the array structures, characterized by typical DRIE scalloping, further confirms controlled release with limited lateral over-etching. Following DRIE release, residual polymeric and inorganic protection layers are removed through a sequential stripping process. O2 plasma ashing first removes fluorocarbon polymer residues generated during the Bosch DRIE cycles. The exposed Cr hard mask and sacrificial Cr sidewall protection layer are then removed using Chromium Etchant 18 at room temperature, with the etch time selected from a calibrated Cr etch rate and an additional overetch margin. Since the NWs are already released after DRIE, the Cr etchant can access the Cr layer from the exposed top, sidewall, and underside regions of the suspended geometry. Finally, HF vapor removes the remaining PECVD SiO2 hard mask, the intermediate SiO2 layer, and the native oxide from the exposed Si surfaces. Vapor HF is used to avoid capillary-force-induced stiction during oxide removal from the released NWs. This sequential O2 plasma/Cr wet etch/vapor HF treatment yields the final suspended Si NW geometry shown in Fig. 1i.

The fabrication was demonstrated at the chip level using batch-compatible cleanroom processes, including optical lithography, PECVD/PVD deposition, plasma etching, DRIE release, and stripping/cleaning. The process does not require serial NW placement, transfer printing, individual device assembly, or manual manipulation of released nanostructures, supporting its scalability toward R&D and pilot-line fabrication. Statistical analysis is performed on the overall 20 NWs per geometry from 3 chips, using 100 sampling points per NW to estimate LER, thereby confirming dimensional reproducibility across multiple released structures. For SOI-based devices, resistance statistics from repeated measurements on single NWs and NW arrays are used to assess fabrication performance and reproducibility. Wafer-level yield qualification would require extended process-control studies beyond the scope of the present work.

The fabrication of suspended sub-100 nm Si NWs without furnace-based thermal processing posed a central challenge, as conventional oxidation and LPCVD steps are crucial for sidewall protection but can contribute to residual-stress development and constrain process integration due to their high thermal budgets. This work addressed that challenge by introducing conformal metallic passivation as a furnace-free alternative, enabling reproducible fabrication of single-crystal NWs with line-widths down to 50 nm, aspect ratios up to 100, and scalable array pitches of 5μm. The process is then extended to SOI substrates to realize two-terminal single-NW and NW-array devices, as well as FET architectures, with electrical measurements confirming predictable resistive and transistor responses, and hydrogen sensitivity at sub-10 nW operating power in two-terminal single-NW devices via nominal 2 nm Pd functionalization. Finally, hybrid M&NEMS relies on additional Si deposition steps, such as epitaxial growth or doped poly-Si formation, to integrate Si NWs with MEMS, which typically involve high-temperature processing. Reducing this thermal budget is therefore important for simplifying the fabrication and minimizing intrinsic stresses in suspended Si NWs\(^{44}\). In addition, furnace-based processing limits process flexibility because it requires ultraclean, metal- and polymer-free substrates to avoid contamination.

The low-thermal-budget process avoids furnace-based oxidation or deposition steps that can introduce intrinsic stress in suspended Si NWs. However, residual stress is not directly quantified in the present sub-100 nm NW devices. The absence of visible sagging, buckling, or deformation during SEM inspection is therefore interpreted as evidence of structural integrity after release, rather than as a quantitative measure of stress. Previous studies have shown that intrinsic stress in suspended Si NWs can arise from fabrication and surface effects, including native-oxide formation, and that its quantification requires dedicated Raman, resonant, or calibrated nanomechanical measurements\(^{44,48,65,66}\). Accordingly, quantitative residual-stress characterization of the present sub-100 nm NWs is left for future dedicated mechanical studies.

Abstract
Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) are versatile one-dimensional building blocks for gas and biochemical sensors, MEMS/NEMS
physical transduction platforms, and integrated electronic devices because of their high surface-to-volume ratios and
compatibility with semiconductor processing. A key limitation of conventional top-down fabrication is its reliance on
furnace-based high-temperature steps, such as thermal oxidation and LPCVD, which can induce residual stress and
constrain post-CMOS integration because of thermal-budget limits above \( 400\,^\circ C \). Here, we present a furnace-free, low-

uniformity, structural stability, and scalability confirm the robustness of the fabrication process for integrated device architectures. Overall, the results demonstrate the functionality of the fabricated NWs across single-NW, array, and transistor configurations on SOI substrates, supporting their use in chemiresistive gas and biochemical sensing after surface functionalization\(^{10,56,64}\). A central feature of the developed approach is the elimination of furnace-based high-temperature steps, such as thermal oxidation and LPCVD, commonly used in conventional suspended NW fabrication. These steps can introduce residual stress in nanoscale beams and impose stringent contamination constraints, as they require ultraclean substrates. In contrast, the present process uses sputtered Cr for sidewall passivation, enabling high etch selectivity during DRIE while maintaining a low thermal budget. The present work builds on the conceptual framework of SCREAM-based single-crystal Si micromachining, while addressing a different dimensional and thermal-budget regime. The original SCREAM I process enabled low-temperature fabrication of suspended single-crystal Si MEMS using RIE-based patterning, sidewall protection, and metallization, with micrometer-scale beam widths and process temperatures below 300 °C\(^{36}\). MacDonald later demonstrated the broader capability of SCREAM for high-aspect-ratio released single-crystal Si MEMS with micrometer-scale minimum features and millimeter-scale suspension spans\(^{45}\). Related MacDonald-group work further demonstrated sub-micron/nanometer-scale Si tips, filaments, and fibers integrated with microinstrumentation; however, those studies relied on oxidation-based size reduction or focused on material and electromechanical characterization rather than furnace-free sub-100 nm Si NW device fabrication\(^{46,47}\).
